Q: Google sheets errors while trying to create dynamic search A:

An { array expression } collects ranges into a virtual array, which means that you cannot refer to its columns with column labels like A. To make it work, replace A with Col1.

Array expressions can be tricky to debug, so it's usually easier to use the the vstack() function. It gets a similar virtual array without requiring carefully placed ;,\ delimiters.

To avoid issues with query column type, get the header row 'Bin 1'!A1:C1 just once, and in subsequent references use 'Bin 2'!A2:C and so on.

The expression select \* is using an incorrect syntax. Use select * or leave out the whole select clause. In a query statement, all clauses are optional, including select.

Putting that together:

=query(
  vstack('Bin 1'!A1:C, 'Bin 2'!A2:C, 'Bin 3'!A2:C, 'Bin 4'!A2:C, 'Bin 5'!A2:C, 'Bin 6'!A2:C, 'Bin 7'!A2:C, 'Bin 8'!A2:C, 'Bin 9'!A2:C, 'Bin 10'!A2:C, 'Bin 11'!A2:C, 'Bin 12'!A2:C, 'Bin 13'!A2:C, 'Bin 14'!A2:C, 'Bin 15'!A2:C, 'Bin 16'!A2:C, 'Bin 17'!A2:C, 'Bin 18'!A2:C, 'Bin 19'!A2:C, 'Bin 20'!A2:C, 'Bin 21'!A2:C, 'Bin 22'!A2:C, 'Bin 23'!A2:C, 'Bin 24'!A2:C, 'Bin 25'!A2:C, 'Bin 26'!A2:C, 'Bin 27'!A2:C, 'Bin 28'!A2:C, 'Bin 29'!A2:C, 'Bin 30'!A2:C, 'Bin 31'!A2:C, 'Bin 32'!A2:C), 
  "where lower(Col1) contains '" & lower(A2) & "' ", 
  1
)

To collect data from a larger number of sheets, not all of which may not exist yet, use the stackSheets_ pattern, like this:

=let(
  stackSheets_,lambda(sheet_names, rangeA1, headers, reduce(headers,sheet_names,lambda(α,β,let(γ,indirect(β&"!"&rangeA1),δ,filter(γ,row(γ)<=max(index(row(γ)*iferror(γ<>"")))),if(counta(iferror(δ)),vstack(α,hstack(byrow(δ,lambda(_,β)),δ)),α))))),

  sheets, arrayformula("Bin " & sequence(100)),
  data, stackSheets_(sheets, "A2:C", { "Sheet name", 'Bin 1'!A1:C1 }),
  query(data, "where lower(Col1) contains '" & lower(A2) & "' ", 1)
)

The formula will get data from 'Bin 1' to 'Bin 100', ignoring sheets that don't exist yet.

See Query Language Reference and vstack().

Q: Geographic plotting A:

Create a list of Patches (for polygons) and Line2D (for points and lines) and pass them to legend:

import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
import matplotlib.lines as mlines
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import geopandas as gpd

#Create three geodataframes from WKT strings stored in lists.
points = ["POINT (18.04538 59.32689)", "POINT (18.09599 59.30791)"]
lines = ["LINESTRING (18.02005 59.31730, 18.10860 59.32257)"]
polygons = ["POLYGON ((18.07049 59.31784, 18.06063 59.30690, 18.09853 59.31472, 18.07049 59.31784))"]
point_df = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.GeoSeries().from_wkt(data=points, crs=4326))
line_df = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.GeoSeries().from_wkt(data=lines, crs=4326))
poly_df = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=gpd.GeoSeries().from_wkt(data=polygons, crs=4326))


#Create Line2Ds and patches with the styling you later plot with
blue_point = mlines.Line2D([], [], color="blue", linewidth=0, markersize=10, marker="o", label="blue point")
red_line = mlines.Line2D([], [], color="red", linewidth=2, label="red line")
green_poly = mpatches.Patch(color="green", label="green polygon")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,1,figsize=(10, 6))

poly_df.plot(ax=ax, color="green", zorder=1)
line_df.plot(ax=ax, color="red", linewidth=2, zorder=2)
point_df.plot(ax=ax, color="blue", markersize=10, marker="o")
ax.legend(handles = [blue_point, red_line, green_poly])

Q: How to iterate over a number in bash through one variable and assign output to a variable? A:

I suggest with minor changes to your code:

#!/bin/bash

read -p "Enter number of keywords: " keywords_num

keywords_total=()

for ((i=1; i<=keywords_num; i++)); do
  read -p "Enter keyword $i: " keyword  # fixed
  keywords_total+=("$keyword")          # fixed
done

declare -p keywords_total
echo "${keywords_total[@]}"

Q: CS50 pset6 readability with python A:

In analyzing this code and reviewing the good comments, I added a diagnostic print statement to go with the statistics currently printed out by the program.

def letters(text):
    chars = 0 
    print("Length:", len(text)) # Diagnostic print of full string length
    for i in range(len(text)):
        if text[i].isalpha:     # Incorrect function call
            chars += 1
    return chars

With that, the program was run and a text sample from the Harvard class was entered and evaluated.

craig@Vera:~/Python_Programs/Grade$ python3 CS50_Grade.py 
Text: Harry Potter was a highly unusual boy in many ways. For one thing, he hated the summer holidays more than any other time of year. For another, he really wanted to do his homework, but was forced to do it in secret, in the dead of the night. And he also happened to be a wizard.
Length: 277
Total words: 56 
Total sentences: 4 
Total characters: 277
11  <-- should be 5

In reviewing the use of the identifying alphabetical characters per the good comments, the python statement should be "if text[i].isalpha():"

def letters(text):
    chars = 0 
    print("Length:", len(text))
    for i in range(len(text)):
        if text[i].isalpha():   # Corrected statement
            chars += 1
    return chars

With that, a retest of the code provided the expected grade value per the Harvard samples.

craig@Vera:~/Python_Programs/Grade$ python3 CS50_Grade.py 
Text: Harry Potter was a highly unusual boy in many ways. For one thing, he hated the summer holidays more than any other time of year. For another, he really wanted to do his homework, but was forced to do it in secret, in the dead of the night. And he also happened to be a wizard.
Length: 277
Total words: 56 
Total sentences: 4 
Total characters: 214
5

The takeaway would be to delve further into python tutorials, especially in the proper formulation and syntax of python functions.
